# 1. History of Backpropagation

## 1.1 Timeline of Key Developments

```
1960s-1970s: Foundation
├── 1960: Henry J. Kelley develops "continuous backpropagation" (optimal control theory)
├── 1970: Seppo Linnainmaa publishes general method for automatic differentiation
└── 1974: Paul Werbos mentions backprop in his PhD thesis (neural networks context)

1980s: Maturation
├── 1986: Rumelhart, Hinton, Williams publish "Learning representations by 
│         back-propagating errors" - popularized backprop
├── 1989: Yann LeCun applies backprop to CNNs (LeNet)
└── 1989: Cybenko proves universal approximation theorem

1990s: Extensions
├── 1998: LeCun et al. publish gradient-based learning applied to document recognition
└── 1998: Hochreiter & Schmidhuber identify vanishing gradient problem

2010s: Deep Learning Revolution
├── 2012: AlexNet wins ImageNet (reignites interest)
├── 2015: ResNet (152 layers - enabled by residual connections)
└── 2017: Adam optimizer becomes dominant

2020s: Modern Era
├── Foundation of modern LLMs (transformers use backprop extensively)
└── Continued research on optimization and gradient flow
```

## 1.2 Key Historical Figures

| Researcher | Year | Contribution |
|------------|------|--------------|
| Seppo Linnainmaa | 1970 | General reverse-mode automatic differentiation |
| Paul Werbos | 1974 | Backprop in neural network context |
| David Rumelhart | 1986 | Popularized backprop algorithm |
| Geoffrey Hinton | 1986 | Co-developed backprop framework |
| Yann LeCun | 1989 | Backprop for CNNs |
| Yoshua Bengio | 1994 | Vanishing gradient problem analysis |

## 1.3 The "Dark Ages" of Neural Networks

During 1995-2010, neural networks were largely abandoned in favor of:
- Support Vector Machines (SVMs)
- Kernel Methods
- Ensemble Methods (Random Forests)

The vanishing gradient problem made training deep networks practically impossible.

## 2.1 Chain Rule Foundation

The backpropagation algorithm is essentially **reverse-mode automatic differentiation** applied to neural networks. At its core is the **chain rule of calculus**.

### Single Variable Chain Rule

```
If: y = f(g(x))
Then: dy/dx = f'(g(x)) · g'(x)
```
